paragraphs: The second charge against the House of Representatives is that it will be too small to have a proper knowledge of the interests of its constituents.

This objection plainly comes from comparing the proposed number of representatives with the great extent of the United States, the number of its inhabitants and the diversity of their interests. It overlooks the circumstances that will distinguish Congress from other legislative bodies. The best answer I can give, then, is a brief explanation of those peculiarities.

It is a sound and important principle that a representative ought to be acquainted with the interests and circumstances of his constituents. But this principle extends only to those circumstances and interests that fall within the authority and care of the representative. Ignorance of a great many minute and particular matters that lie outside the reach of legislation is consistent with every quality needed to carry out the legislative trust properly. To determine how much information is required for exercising a particular authority, we must therefore look to the objects that fall within that authority.
What are the objects of federal legislation? Those of greatest importance, and those that seem to require the most local knowledge, are commerce, taxation and the militia.

A proper regulation of commerce requires a great deal of information, as I have remarked elsewhere. But so far as that information concerns the laws and local situation of each individual State, a very few representatives would be quite sufficient to carry it to the federal councils.

Taxation will consist, in great measure, of duties that will be bound up with the regulation of commerce, and to that extent the preceding remark applies here as well. So far as taxation consists of internal collections, a more widespread knowledge of the circumstances of the State may be needed. But will not a very few intelligent men, elected from across the State, possess this knowledge in sufficient degree? Divide the largest State into ten or twelve districts, and you will find that no district has any peculiar local interests that the representative of that district will not know. Besides this source of information, the laws of the State, framed by representatives from every part of it, will be almost sufficient of themselves as a guide. In every State, regulations on this subject have been made, and must continue to be made, that will in many cases leave the federal legislature little more to do than review the different laws and combine them in one general act. A skillful individual in his study, with all the local codes before him, might draw up a law on some subjects of taxation for the whole Union without any help from oral information. And it may be expected that whenever internal taxes are necessary, and particularly in cases requiring uniformity throughout the States, the simpler objects will be preferred. To appreciate fully how much the State codes will ease this branch of federal legislation, we need only suppose for a moment that this State, or any other, were divided into a number of parts, each having and exercising within itself a power of local legislation. Is it not evident that the several volumes of their proceedings would hold a good deal of local information and preparatory labor, which would greatly shorten the work of the general legislature and make a much smaller number of members sufficient for it? The federal councils will gain a great advantage from another circumstance as well. The representatives of each State will bring with them not only a considerable knowledge of its laws and a local knowledge of their own districts. They will also probably in all cases have been members, and may even at that very time be members, of the State legislature, where all the local information and interests of the State are gathered, and from which they may easily be carried by a very few hands into the legislature of the United States.

(What I have said about taxation applies with even greater force to the militia. For however much the rules of discipline may differ among the States, they are the same throughout each particular State, and they depend on circumstances that can differ but little in different parts of the same State.)(E1)

(With regard to the regulation of the militia, there are scarcely any circumstances in which local knowledge can be called necessary. The general face of the country, whether mountainous or level, and most suited to the operations of infantry or cavalry, is almost the only consideration of this kind that can arise. The art of war teaches general principles of organization, movement and discipline, which apply everywhere.)(E1)

The attentive reader will see that the reasoning used here to prove that a moderate number of representatives is sufficient does not in any way contradict what I argued on another occasion about the extensive information representatives ought to have and the time it may take to acquire it. Where this information concerns local objects, it is made necessary and difficult not by differences of laws and local circumstances within a single State, but by differences among different States. Taking each State by itself, its laws are the same and its interests are only slightly varied. A few men, therefore, will have all the knowledge needed to represent it properly. If the interests and affairs of each individual State were perfectly simple and uniform, knowing them in one part would mean knowing them in every other, and a single member taken from any part of the State could represent the whole of it competently. When we compare the different States with one another, we find great dissimilarity in their laws and in many other circumstances connected with the objects of federal legislation, all of which the federal representatives ought to know something about. So while a few representatives from each State may bring with them a proper knowledge of their own State, every representative will have much to learn about all the other States. The changes of time, as I remarked before, will have an assimilating effect on the comparative situation of the different States. The effect of time on the internal affairs of the States taken singly will be just the opposite. At present some of the States are little more than a society of farmers, and few of them have made much progress in those branches of industry that give variety and complexity to the affairs of a nation. These, however, will in every one of them be the fruits of a more advanced population, and will require a fuller representation on the part of each State. The foresight of the Convention has accordingly provided that the growth of population may be accompanied by a proper increase in the representative branch of the government.

The experience of Great Britain, which offers mankind so many political lessons, both warnings and examples, and which has often been consulted in the course of these inquiries, confirms the conclusion we have just reached. The number of inhabitants in the two kingdoms of England and Scotland cannot be put at less than eight million. The representatives of these eight million in the House of Commons number five hundred and fifty-eight. Of these, one ninth are elected by three hundred and sixty-four persons, and one half by five thousand seven hundred and twenty-three persons.(1) It cannot be supposed that the half thus elected, who do not even live among the people at large, can add anything either to the people's security against the government or to the legislative councils' knowledge of the people's circumstances and interests. On the contrary, it is notorious that they are more often the representatives and instruments of the executive than the guardians and advocates of the people's rights. They might therefore, with great propriety, be considered as something more than a mere deduction from the real representatives of the nation. We will, however, consider them in that light alone, and will not extend the deduction to a considerable number of others who do not live among their constituents, are only faintly connected with them and have very little particular knowledge of their affairs. With all these concessions, only two hundred and seventy-nine persons will be the depository of the safety, interest and happiness of eight million. That is to say, there will be only one representative to uphold the rights and explain the situation of TWENTY-EIGHT THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY constituents, in an assembly exposed to the whole force of executive influence, and extending its authority to every object of legislation in a nation whose affairs are in the highest degree diversified and complicated. Yet it is quite certain, not only that a valuable portion of liberty has been preserved under all these circumstances, but also that the defects in the British code can be blamed only in very small proportion on the legislature's ignorance of the circumstances of the people. Giving this case the weight it deserves, and comparing it with that of the House of Representatives as explained above, it seems to give the fullest assurance that one representative for every THIRTY THOUSAND INHABITANTS will make the House both a safe and a competent guardian of the interests that will be entrusted to it.
E1. Two versions of this paragraph appear in different editions.
